newsitem.title: CHINA: China approves plan to gut HK civil liberties laws.
newsitem.headline: China approves plan to gut HK civil liberties laws.

text.p: China has approved plans to abolish a series of Hong Kong laws, including parts of those protecting civil liberties in the territory, in a move that has sparked cries of protest from Britain.

The standing committee of the National People's Congress, China's parliament, published a list of 25 Hong Kong laws that will be amended or scrapped when Beijing takes control of the British colony on July 1, the official Xinhua news agency reported on Sunday.

Among the laws targeted are Hong Kong's Bill of Rights and ordinances allowing the formation of political parties and the holding of peaceful demonstrations -- key parts of London's attempt to lock in a democratic framework before handing Hong Kong to its new communist rulers.

British officials and democratic activists in Hong Kong have blasted the Chinese plan as an attempt to gut civil liberties for the territory's 6.3 million people, who after July 1 will be citizens of a "Special Administrative Region" of China.
Tung Chee-hwa, who will take over as Hong Kong's first post-colonial leader, has defended the changes as "striking the right balance between individual rights and social order".

Xinhua said the parliamentary standing committee sought to change only legal measures "considered to be contradictory" to the Basic Law, which China promulgated in 1990 to serve as Hong Kong's constitution.
The move is a final slap at London, which provoked Chinese anger by pushing through a series of democratic changes for the colony in the last years of British rule.
China has already set up a provisional legislature to take over from the elected Legislative Council, and has vowed to dismantle other reforms including provisions for democratic elections.
Beijing has brushed away protests from London and Washington, saying that after July 1 Hong Kong will be purely an internal affair of China.
